name: Aranyasundareswarar Temple, Keezhai Tirukkattuppalli
deity: Shiva as Aranyasundareswarar (Aranyeswarar), with the goddess Akilandeswari
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kaveri delta, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); the present structure is later and not firmly dated
dynasty: Medieval patrons of the Chola country (specific dynasty not firmly sourced)
summary: Aranyasundareswarar, the beautiful Lord of the forest, is a quiet Tevaram shrine near Tiruvenkadu, praised by Sambandar and remembered as the place where Indra was freed from the guilt of slaying Vritra.

sections.history: Keezhai Tirukkattuppalli lies in the green delta of the Kaveri, about two kilometres west of Tiruvenkadu, in the Sirkazhi country of Mayiladuthurai district. In the Tevaram it is simply Tirukkattuppalli, and the saint Tirugnanasambandar sang a decad of hymns to its Lord, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam and one of the Tevaram shrines on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The prefix Keezhai, meaning lower or downstream, sets it apart from the other Tirukkattuppalli higher up the river. The name Aranya, the forest, recalls a time when this whole countryside was woodland, and the shrine has been kept in worship for well over a thousand years, its present form built up by the patrons of the Chola country across the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple makes no show from the road. There is no towering gopuram; the entrance opens straight into a spacious outer prakaram, and the quiet of that wide enclosure is part of the shrine's character. In the sanctum the Lord is a swayambhu linga, self-manifested, set upon a square avudayar beneath a two-tiered vimana of the dwidala form. The goddess Akilandeswari has her shrine to the left of the Lord, so that devotees can behold the divine pair from a single place. Temple accounts also speak of seven lingas within the precincts, one of them unusual in carrying two banas.
sections.legends: The old story belongs to Indra, king of the gods. He slew Vishwaroopa, and when the young man's father raised the demon Vritra in vengeance, Indra killed him too, using the thunderbolt fashioned from the spine of the sage Dadhichi. The deed lay on him as the heavy sin of brahmahatti, and his guru advised him to seek Shiva. Indra came to this forest, worshipped the Lord with penance, and was cleansed of his guilt. From that forest the Lord took the names Aranyeswarar, Lord of the forest, and Aranyasundareswarar, the beautiful Lord of the forest. The temple keeps the memory of a Lord who frees even the mighty from the weight of their deeds.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in February or March is the great night of worship here. Skanda Sashti in the month of Aippasi (October–November), Arudra Darshan in Margazhi (December–January) and Vinayaka Chaturthi in August or September are also celebrated, and the monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come here for stillness rather than spectacle. With no great tower to announce it, the temple reveals itself slowly: a wide, open courtyard, the self-manifested linga in the sanctum, and the goddess Akilandeswari close at the Lord's left hand. The shrine stands among delta fields only a short way from the famous Swetaranyeswarar temple of Tiruvenkadu, and the two are easily visited together on one morning. Devotees who feel the weight of past wrongs hold this place dear as the sanctuary where Indra himself found release.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the early evening, with a long midday break; published timings are roughly 8:00–11:00 and 18:00–19:30. Confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally tolerated in the outer prakaram but not inside the sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple custom. Ask the priest or temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is about 2 km west of Tiruvenkadu on the road towards Elayamuthukulapuram, and roughly 13 km from Sirkazhi, the nearest railway station. Mayiladuthurai is a larger railway junction in the region, and Tiruchirappalli and Chennai are the main airports. Local buses run to Tiruvenkadu; an auto-rickshaw or taxi from Sirkazhi or Tiruvenkadu is the easiest way to reach the temple itself.
